title: Structured output and tool use
summary: How to get data your code can trust out of a model with JSON schemas, and how tool use lets the model ask your code to look things up or act.
youWillLearn: Why parsing free text from a model breaks, and how a JSON schema fixes it
Why a valid shape still needs checking before it reaches your database
How tool use works: the model asks, your code runs, the model answers
Why the model must never decide whose data a tool touches

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.JSON: A plain-text format for data that code reads easily: names and values in curly braces, lists in square brackets.
glossary.structured output: Asking the API for an answer that must match a schema you define, so your code gets clean data instead of prose.
glossary.JSON schema: A description of the shape JSON must have: which fields, which types, which are required.
glossary.Zod: A popular TypeScript library for describing data shapes once and using them for both types and runtime checks.
glossary.tool use: Also called function calling: you describe functions to the model, and it can reply with a request to call one, with arguments.
glossary.tool_use: The content block a model returns when it wants a tool called: the tool's name, an id, and the input arguments.
glossary.tool_result: The content block you send back with the output of a tool call, matched to the request by its id.
glossary.session: The server's record of who is logged in, tied to the browser's sign-in cookie. Code reads the current user from it.
glossary.RLS: Row Level Security: Postgres rules that decide which rows each logged-in user may read or change, enforced by the database itself.

steps.title: Notely learns to find tasks
body: Maya, a Notely user, wants the to-dos pulled out of her notes. Claude Code built it: the app server (the computer running Notely's code) sends the note to the Claude API (Anthropic's AI) with "Return the tasks as JSON" (a plain-text data format code can read).
It saves each task in the database, where notes live.

scene.caption: Note in, tasks out, saved to the database.

steps.title: "Sure! Here are your tasks:"
body: Nine times in ten it works. The tenth reply starts with "Sure! Here are your tasks:", or wraps the data in extra formatting, and the code that reads it (JSON.parse) throws an error.
No tasks get saved, and Maya sees a broken button. Free text is for people, not for code.
changes: ~ Parse errors 0 → 10 in every 100
~ App Server: cannot read the reply
~ Database: nothing saved

scene.caption: A friendly sentence in front of the data breaks the code that reads it.

steps.title: Hand the model a form to fill in
body: Instead of asking nicely, give the API a JSON schema: the exact fields, their types, which ones are required.
With structured output turned on, the API holds the answer to that shape. No greeting, no extra formatting, no missing bracket. Whenever the answer finishes normally, your code gets data it can read.

callout.text: Asking a guest to "write down your details" on a blank page, versus handing them a form with labeled boxes. Same person, far more usable result.

changes: + Schema: the exact shape the answer must have
~ Parse errors 10 → 0
~ App Server and Database working again

scene.caption: The schema goes with the request, and the API keeps the answer to it.

steps.title: One schema for your code and the API
body: In TypeScript (the language Notely is written in), Zod lets you describe the shape once. The SDK (Anthropic's helper library) turns it into a JSON schema for the request, and checks the reply against it.
You get back parsed_output: a typed object, not a string. Your editor knows tasks[0].title exists before you run anything.

code.caption: zodOutputFormat comes from @anthropic-ai/sdk/helpers/zod. A cut-off or refused answer will not fit the schema, so check stop_reason first.

changes: ~ Schema: written once in Zod, used by code and API
~ App Server: gets a typed object back

scene.caption: One description of the shape serves both your code and the API.

steps.title: Right shape, wrong facts
body: A schema guarantees the shape, not the truth. The due date can be a valid date the note never mentioned. A task can be invented.
So the app server checks the content before saving: is the date real and in the future, is the title non-empty, is this task already saved? Then it inserts, as the logged-in user.

callout.text: Keep schemas small and flat. Prefer null for "unknown" over a guessed value, and say so in the field's description.

changes: ~ App Server: checks every task before saving
~ Schema steps back

scene.caption: Between the model and the database sits a check on the content.

steps.title: Tools: the model asks, your code acts
body: Now Notely gets a chat. Maya asks: "When is the logo due?" The model does not have her notes. It needs to look.

With tool use, you describe functions it may request, like search_notes. Instead of answering, the model can reply "please run search_notes for 'logo deadline'". Your code runs it. The model never touches your database.
changes: − Schema: we move on to the chat
+ search_notes: a tool your code runs on request
~ App Server: back to normal

scene.caption: The model asks for a search; the app server runs it against the database.

steps.title: The round trip, step by step
body: The app server sends the question plus the tool list. The reply says stop_reason: "tool_use" and holds a tool_use block. Your code runs the search and sends the output back as a tool_result with the same id. Then the model answers.
Two model calls. The API has no memory, so call two re-sends the whole conversation.

code.caption: The id links the result to the request. Then the model answers: "Friday."

changes: ~ Model calls 1 → 2 a turn
~ Claude API: answers "Friday" from the search result

scene.caption: Ask, run, send back, answer: two calls to the model.

steps.title: Defining Notely's search tool
body: A tool is a name, a description and an input schema. The description is a prompt: it tells the model when to use the tool, so write it like one.
strict: true holds the arguments to the schema exactly. Notice what is missing: any user id. The app server already knows who is logged in.

code.caption: Lesson 5 shows how search_notes finds notes by meaning, not only by keyword.

changes: ~ search_notes: takes only a query, no user id

scene.caption: The tool's only input is what to look for.

steps.title: The model must not pick whose data
body: Tool arguments come from the model, which reads user text. If search_notes took a user_id, crafted text could ask for someone else's notes.
So take identity from the session (the server's record of who is logged in), never from the model. Query as that user, so RLS (database rules: each user sees only their rows) applies.

callout.text: Read every tool's input_schema: any user_id, email or table name? Does the handler use the service role key, which skips RLS? Are tool errors sent back with is_error: true? Does anything destructive run without a confirm?

changes: + Someone Else: sends a message asking for user 7's notes
~ search_notes, bad version: takes a user_id from the model
~ Database: hands over another user's notes

scene.caption: If the model picks the user id, crafted text picks it for you.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: When code needs the answer, ask for structured output against a schema, then check the content before saving.

When the model needs to look something up or act, give it tools. It replies with a request; your code decides, runs it as the logged-in user, and sends back the result. The model asks. Your code is in charge.
changes: − Someone Else
~ search_notes: user comes from the session
~ Database: RLS shows only Maya's rows

scene.caption: The model asks, your code runs the tool as Maya, the database guards the rows.

quiz.question: Claude Code extracts tasks with "Return JSON only" in the prompt and JSON.parse on the reply. It fails now and then. What is the sturdier fix?

options.text: Add "ONLY JSON, NO OTHER TEXT" in capitals.
options.why: That lowers the failure rate but cannot guarantee it. A schema-constrained answer can.

options.text: Strip everything before the first { with a regex.
options.why: That patches one failure style and misses others, like cut-off or slightly malformed JSON.

options.text: Use structured output with a schema, and read parsed_output.
options.why: The API holds the answer to the schema, so every completed answer parses into the right shape. Prompt wording alone cannot promise that.

quiz.question: In tool use, who actually runs search_notes?

options.text: Your server code, after the model asks for it.
options.why: The model only returns a tool_use request. Your code decides whether to run it, runs it, and returns a tool_result.

options.text: The model, by connecting to your database.
options.why: The model has no access to your systems. It can only ask your code to do things.

options.text: The provider's servers, using your database password.
options.why: For tools you define, the provider never runs anything on your behalf. You hold the keys and run the code.

quiz.question: A tool Claude Code wrote is get_notes(user_id), and the handler uses the service role key. What is the risk?

options.text: None, because the model is told to use the current user's id.
options.why: Instructions can be overridden by crafted input. Security cannot depend on the model following the rules.

options.text: It is slower, because each call carries a user id.
options.why: Speed is not the problem. Letting model output choose whose data to read is.

options.text: Crafted text can make the model request another user's id, and nothing in the database stops it.
options.why: The model picks the argument and the service role skips RLS. Take the user from the session and query as that user.

takeaways: Code needs data, not prose. Use structured output with a schema instead of parsing free text.
A schema guarantees shape, not truth. Check dates, duplicates and content before you save.
With tool use, the model only asks. Your code runs the tool and returns a tool_result.
Write tool descriptions like prompts: say when to use the tool.
Never let tool arguments choose identity. Take the user from the session and let RLS limit the rows.
